title: The museum opens its source

summary.text: Two Commodores joined the gallery, both picked after a survey of the *8-bit* and *16-bit* home-computer field. The [VIC-20](station:vic20) came first, and there is charmingly little to it: open the page and you are looking at the same friendly BASIC screen a child saw on a shop shelf, cursor blinking, ready for you to type. The [Plus/4](station:plus4) followed, the odder of the pair — Commodore built an office suite into the machine itself, so **3-PLUS-1** (a word processor, a spreadsheet and a card-file program) is there the instant it powers on, with one-tap buttons on the on-screen keyboard to reach each one. On its first day the Plus/4 opened mid-spreadsheet, which rather gave the game away; it now starts where the real machine starts, on the power-on screen that says "3-PLUS-1 ON KEY F1".

On 7 August the <u>museum's source code went public</u>. Everything behind the gallery — the site you click through, the software that streams each machine to your browser, and the recipes that build the machines themselves — is now open for anyone to read, learn from, or run themselves, under the MIT licence, with the streaming code under GPL-2.0-or-later. The changes the museum makes to **MAME** and **QEMU** to keep old machines happy are published as public branches too, rather than hidden. A source link now sits in the gallery footer and on the sign-in page, so you can go from a running machine to the code that runs it in one click. Each machine's page also grew a carousel of photographs of the real hardware: over a hundred freely-licensed pictures, every one credited to its photographer. Then someone opened each picture at full size and read its caption — a "tower-case system" turned out to be plainly a laptop. Every caption is now written from the photograph you are actually looking at, and portrait pictures no longer arrive lying on their side.

A visitor's typed-in program came back scrambled on the VIC-20, which turned out to be the museum typing faster than the machine could listen. Demonstrations now type at a pace each machine can keep up with, measured against that machine rather than guessed — a fix that also caught the [Amstrad CPC](station:amstradcpc) quietly rushing since the day it opened. And [IRIX](station:irix) now opens on a working desktop, icons and toolchest and all, instead of a login screen.

bullets: The VIC-20 still greets a visitor the way it greeted a shopper: CBM BASIC V2, and 3583 BYTES FREE — every byte an unexpanded machine had
The *Commodore* key exists on no modern keyboard and on no phone at all, so the Plus/4's on-screen keyboard carries a labelled one of its own
Neither Commodore needs a cartridge or a disk: the emulator already carries their ROMs, the whole of **3-PLUS-1** included
IRIX types its own login one keystroke per tick — any faster and the machine panics before it ever reaches the desktop
The photographs on the [Windows NT 3.51](station:nt351) page are *DEC AlphaStations*: NT ran on far more than beige *x86* boxes
[9front](station:ninefront)'s page shows the Bell Labs it descends from — the *DMD 5620* terminal, Thompson and Ritchie, and Glenda, licensed by her creator
Period advertising is linked, never copied: an *AlphaServer* brochure and a television advert for [OS/2 Warp](station:os2warp)
One picture on the [Windows 95](station:win95) page showed a *386/16*, a machine below the floor **Windows 95** itself demands; it was replaced
Every gallery image is cleared against Wikimedia's own licence record by a script, which caught two invented file titles on its first run
A survey of the *PDP-11* family and of thirty more home computers went into the notes before any of them got a page
